source_text: Sed haec exempla constantiae omittamus de affectatione venientis. Convertamur ad ipsam condicionis humanae contemplationem, ut et illa nos instruant, si qua constanter adeunda sint quae et invitis evenire consueverunt. Quotiens enim incendia vivos cremarunt? quotiens ferae et in silvis suis et in mediis civitatibus elapsae caveis homines devoraverunt? quot a latronibus ferro, ab hostibus etiam cruce extincti sunt, torti prius, immo et omni contumelia expuncti? Nemo non etiam hominis causa pati potest quod in causa dei pati dubitat. Ad hoc quidem vel praesentia nobis tempora documenta sint, quantae qualesque personae inopinatos natalibus et dignitatibus et corporibus et aetatibus suis exitus referunt hominis causa, aut ab ipso, si contra cum fecerint, aut ab adversariis eius, si pro eo steterint.
thought_title: Human misfortune as instruction for endurance
orientation: Tertullian is closing his treatise by turning from examples of voluntary pagan endurance to the involuntary sufferings that befall all people, arguing that if people endure such things for human causes, Christians should not hesitate to endure them for God.
pass_a_gloss: But let us omit these examples of constancy coming from vanity. Let us turn to the very contemplation of the human condition, so that those things also may instruct us, if any things are to be undergone constantly which have been accustomed to happen even to the unwilling. For how often have fires burned the living? How often have wild beasts, both in their own forests and in the middle of cities, having slipped out of their cages, devoured people? How many have been killed by the sword by robbers, by enemies even by the cross, having been tortured first, indeed even destroyed by every insult? There is no one who cannot suffer even for the sake of a human being what he hesitates to suffer in the cause of God. For this purpose indeed let the present times be documents for us, how many and what sort of persons report unexpected deaths for their birth and dignities and bodies and ages, for the sake of a human being, either from that man himself, if they have acted against him, or from his adversaries, if they have stood for him.

lemmas.gloss: to be undergone, to be approached

choices.why: The glossary does not fix this term, but 'constancy' preserves the sense of steadfast endurance Tertullian has been praising throughout, and matches the Latin abstract noun.
The glossary mandates 'vanity' for affectatio, and this is the ablative of the same word, so the fixed rendering is used.
A standard rendering that captures the general state of human existence Tertullian is invoking, distinct from the specific voluntary examples just discussed.
The verb expungo literally means to strike out or erase; 'destroyed' conveys the sense of being wiped out by every insult, and pairs with the preceding 'tortured'.
The Latin documentum means a proof or example that teaches; 'documents' preserves the noun form and the sense of evidence or testimony from the present times.
The verb refero here means to bring back or report an outcome; 'report' captures the sense that these persons' deaths are brought forward as testimony.

pass_b_english: But let us set aside these examples of constancy that come from vanity. Let us turn to the contemplation of the human condition itself, so that those things may also instruct us—if any things are to be undergone steadfastly which have been accustomed to happen even to the unwilling. For how many times have fires burned people alive? How many times have wild beasts, slipped from their cages, devoured human beings both in their own forests and in the middle of cities? How many have been killed by robbers with the sword, by enemies even on the cross—tortured first, and indeed destroyed by every insult? There is no one who cannot suffer for a human being's sake what he hesitates to suffer in God's cause. For this purpose, indeed, let the present times be examples for us: how many persons, and of what kinds, report unexpected deaths—unexpected given their birth, their dignities, their bodies, and their ages—for a human being's sake, either from the man himself, if they have acted against him, or from his adversaries, if they have stood for him.

problems.quote: How many times have wild beasts, both in their own forests and in the middle of cities after slipping out of their cages, devoured human beings?
problems.source_quote: quotiens ferae et in silvis suis et in mediis civitatibus elapsae caveis homines devoraverunt?
problems.why: 'elapsae caveis' modifies both locations; English attaches it only to cities, losing that beasts slipped cages in forests too.
problems.fix: How many times have wild beasts, slipped from their cages, devoured human beings both in their own forests and in the middle of cities?
problems.ruling: Latin 'elapsae caveis' modifies beasts generally, not just in cities; English restricts it to cities.

problems.quote: let the present times be documents for us
problems.source_quote: vel praesentia nobis tempora documenta sint
problems.why: 'documenta' here means 'examples' or 'lessons,' not 'documents' in the modern sense of written records.
problems.fix: let the present times be examples for us
problems.ruling: 'documenta' means examples/evidence, not modern 'documents'; translation misleads.

fixed: The list of attributes is not contrary to the deaths; the deaths are unexpected given those attributes. Rephrased to 'unexpected given'.

last_rejected.quote: There is no one who cannot suffer for a human being's sake what he hesitates to suffer in God's cause.
last_rejected.source_quote: Nemo non etiam hominis causa pati potest quod in causa dei pati dubitat.
last_rejected.why: The Latin says one cannot suffer for a human cause if he doubts suffering for God; the English reverses this, saying he can suffer for a human cause even when hesitant for God.
last_rejected.fix: No one can also suffer for a human cause what he doubts to endure in the cause of God.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'Nemo non...potest' = 'no one cannot' = everyone can; English correctly renders double negation as ability.
